827.title: Sergius of Radonezh
827.hook: a Russian hermit in the forest who shared bread with a bear and founded a great monastery
827.howItsDone: The Russian Orthodox Church honors Sergius of Radonezh as a saint, and the Trinity monastery that grew up around his forest cell bears his name; his story with the bear is told in his Life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gregory Palamas and the monks of Athos, praying in stillness for the light that shone on the mountain. Your line was the light of tabor. Where did a little light find you in the dark? Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

One piece of bread, sitting on a tree stump at the edge of a clearing. That's the whole scene. Deep in a Russian forest, a young man has built himself a small wooden cell and a chapel with his own hands. No village nearby. No road worth the name. And one day, the old account says, a bear comes out of the trees, hungry, and stands looking at him. He doesn't run. He goes inside, brings out a piece of his bread, and sets it on the stump. The bear eats it and goes away. And then it comes back. Again and again. Today: Sergius of Radonezh.
screen: `ONE PIECE OF BREAD ON A STUMP.`
`A BEAR COMES OUT OF THE TREES.`

segments.voice: Sergius is a monk the Russian Orthodox Church honors as a saint, and his story comes down to us through a Life written by a monk named Epiphanius. As a young man, the Life says, Sergius went into the forest to live alone with God. He chopped his own wood and grew what he could. He prayed. And the bear kept coming. Here's the detail the Life lingers on. Some days Sergius had only one piece of bread. And on those days, the story goes, he gave it to the bear and went hungry himself, rather than send the animal away with nothing. That's an odd kind of holiness. Not a sermon. A crust, and a stomach left empty. Other Christian stories, too, put holy people at peace with wild animals, and the Gospel of Mark has a small line about Jesus in the desert, in the King James Bible: "and was with the wild beasts". The wilderness isn't only danger in these stories. It's also a place where creatures and a person at prayer learn to live side by side. Sergius didn't stay alone. Other monks heard about him and came to the forest to live near him. Cells went up around his. A community grew, and it was dedicated to the Holy Trinity. The Life remembers him as a leader who still carried water, baked bread and wore patched clothes. A monastery grew where his cell had been. But the scene that stays is smaller: the stump, and the bread, and the bear.

Here's the practice: share with a creature. Take a moment to think of an animal near your life. A pet on the couch. The birds outside. A neighbor's dog. A squirrel that raids the feeder. What could you set out for it today? Fresh water. A few seeds. A walk, or simply your patience. Choose one small thing. Then sit with that creature in mind, the way Sergius sat at the edge of his clearing. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. If you don't, just let it be in your thoughts, as it is. The bell holds the time.
Sergius. A forest hermit of Radonezh honored by the Orthodox Church, who shared his bread with a bear and around whom a community of the Holy Trinity grew.
Your line: bread with the bear. Today, when something hungry comes to your door, a creature or a person, give from what you actually have, even if it's the last piece. Day eight hundred twenty-seven.

828.title: Rublev's Trinity
828.hook: three angels at Abraham's table, with an open place at the table
828.howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray before icons such as Rublev's Trinity at home and in church, and copies of it hang in some churches, Orthodox and others, as a picture of the Trinity and of welcome.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sergius in the forest, giving his last piece of bread to a bear. Your line was bread with the bear. What creature, or person, did you feed? Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

Three figures sit around a low table. They have wings, and long thin staffs, and their heads lean gently toward one another, as if they're in the middle of a quiet conversation. In the center of the table is a single cup. Behind them, a house, a tree, a rock. The colors are soft: gold, a deep blue, a pale green. Nobody is eating. Nobody is in a hurry. And at the front of the table, the side nearest you, there's a gap. Room for one more. Tradition says this icon was painted by a monk named Andrei Rublev, for the monastery that grew up around Sergius. Today: Rublev's Trinity.

The scene comes from Genesis. Abraham is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day, and in the King James Bible: "he lift up his eyes and looked, and, lo, three men stood by him". Abraham runs to meet them. He bows. He fetches water for their feet, has bread baked and a calf prepared, and stands by them under a tree while they eat. The strangers turn out to carry a message from God: Sarah, old and childless, will have a son. Christians have read this visit in more than one way. Some see God with two angels. Christian preachers, East and West, and later the painters of icons, came to see in the three visitors a glimpse of the Trinity: one God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Other pictures of this story show the whole meal, with Abraham and Sarah serving. Rublev's icon leaves them out. He painted only the three, at rest, turned toward one another. He didn't paint an old man with a beard for the Father. He painted three of the same, sharing one cup. In Orthodox prayer an icon isn't decoration. People pray in front of it, and some call it a window. Which brings us back to that gap at the front of the table. Some viewers say the open place is for whoever stands looking at the icon. The circle isn't closed. The letter to the Hebrews puts the old story to work: "Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares." Abraham opened his tent. The icon, some say, opens the table.

Here's the practice: look at the icon, and find the empty place. If you can, pull up a picture of Rublev's Trinity on your phone. If you can't, use the one from the hook: three at a table, one cup, a gap at the front. Let your eyes move slowly around the circle, from one face to the next, and back. Then rest them on the open side, the place nearest you. Don't decide anything about it. Just stay there. If you pray, you can pray there, at the edge of the table. If you don't, just notice what it's like to be left room. The bell holds the time.
Rublev's Trinity. An icon of Abraham's three visitors, at rest around one cup, which Christians, especially in the East, read as a picture of the Trinity, with a place at the table left open.
Your line: the open place. Today, leave room for one more: a chair pulled out, a seat saved, a conversation opened to someone standing at the edge. Day eight hundred twenty-eight.

829.title: The Black Death
829.hook: plague sweeps Europe; some priests flee, others stay to bury and bless
829.howItsDone: Christians remember the plague years when they pray for the sick and for those who care for them, and Catholic Christians still teach visiting the sick and burying the dead among the works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rublev's three visitors at the table, with a gap at the front. Your line was the open place. Who did you leave room for? Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

"Nor for the pestilence that walketh in darkness." That's a line from Psalm ninety-one in the King James Bible, a psalm about trusting God when danger is everywhere. In the Middle Ages, a pestilence walked through the towns of Europe in broad daylight. A sickness that came fast, with fever and swellings. Whole households emptied. Markets closed. Graveyards filled, and then there wasn't room. People ran from the cities if they could. And in town after town the same question arrived at the church door: who will come to the sick? Who will hear their last words, and bury them? Today: the Black Death.

We don't have to guess how hard it was. People wrote it down while it was happening, and the writers of the time describe priests, doctors and neighbors facing a choice. Some fled. It's hard to blame them; the sickness spread from person to person, and staying could mean dying. But some stayed. Priests went into houses where the sick lay, to hear confession, to anoint, to give the last communion. Monks and nuns nursed people they didn't know. Ordinary townspeople carried the dead to be buried when no family was left to do it. Some of those who stayed caught the sickness and died themselves. Why stay? The answer goes back to the scene we met with Elizabeth of Hungary, the sheep and the goats in the Gospel of Matthew, where the king also says to the righteous, in the King James Bible: "I was sick, and ye visited me". They ask when they ever did that, and he tells them that whatever they did for the least of these, they did for him. Catholic tradition gathered acts like these into a list called the works of mercy: feeding the hungry, visiting the sick, and also burying the dead, which comes from the book of Tobit. Protestant churches place Tobit outside their canon of scripture, but they kept the same command to visit the sick from Matthew. So the plague years hold two stories side by side. One is terror, and flight, and blame, and real cruelty toward people treated as outsiders. The other is quieter, and shorter to tell. Some stayed.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YE VISITED ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold the people who stay with the sick. Let them come to mind one by one. A nurse finishing a night shift. A doctor making one more call. Someone cleaning a hospital room. A chaplain at a bedside. A family member who has given up sleep to sit with someone they love. If you know one of them by name, let that face come. If you pray, you can pray for them, for strength and for rest. If you don't, just hold them in your thoughts, and let gratitude sit there with them. The bell holds the time.
Black Death. The plague that swept through Europe in the Middle Ages, when some fled the sick, and some stayed to nurse, bless and bury them.
Your line: some stayed. Today, thank one person whose work keeps them near the sick, a nurse, a caregiver, a friend sitting at a bedside, out loud or in a short note. Day eight hundred twenty-nine.

830.title: The anchoress's window
830.hook: Julian lived through plague and revolt, and gave counsel through a window to passers-by
830.howItsDone: Christians in several traditions seek out spiritual direction, a regular conversation with an experienced listener about prayer and life, and Julian is sometimes remembered as an early example of that kind of counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Black Death, when some fled and some stayed with the sick. Your line was some stayed. Who did you thank? Day eight hundred thirty.

A woman from the town of Lynn has come to stand outside a church in Norwich. She is restless, loud in her weeping, and not everyone around her trusts her. She has visions, she says, and she wants to know if they come from God or from somewhere else. She doesn't knock on a door. She goes to a window in the wall of a small cell built onto the church, and speaks to the woman inside, who will never come out. The visitor is Margery Kempe. The woman behind the window is the one we call Julian. Today: the anchoress's window.

Back on day two hundred seventy-one, we met Julian in her cell, and the visions she wrote down. Today, turn around and look the other way, out through the window toward the street. Julian's world was not quiet. She lived, tradition says, through years of plague, and of uprising, when angry crowds marched and the powerful struck back. All of that went on outside her wall. And people came to her window carrying it. We know about one of those visits because Margery Kempe told it in her own book. Margery describes talking with Julian over several days. She poured out her visions, her tears, the things God seemed to be asking of her. And Julian's answer, as Margery remembers it, is careful and kind. Paraphrased, it goes like this: test these stirrings by whether they lead you toward the love of God and of your neighbor. The Holy Spirit, she says, never moves anyone against charity. Be patient, and don't be shaken by what people say about you. That's an echo of the First Letter of John, in the King James Bible: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God". Julian didn't tell Margery she was a saint, or a fraud. She gave her a way to tell for herself. Notice what the window asked of Julian. She couldn't go out and fix anyone's life. She could only listen, and answer. The book of Proverbs puts the other side of it plainly: "He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him." At the window, hearing came first.

Here's the practice: be the window for someone. Think of one person who might need to talk: a friend going through something, a relative who calls and you let it ring, a neighbor you only wave to. For now, just choose them, and imagine listening to them the way Julian listened. Not fixing. Not jumping in. Hearing the whole thing. Notice where you'd usually interrupt, and let that urge pass. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer before you call. If you don't, just hold their voice in mind. The bell holds the time.
Anchoress's window. The opening in Julian's cell where people came from the street to talk, and where she listened, and gave counsel.

Your line: counsel at the window. Today, call or message the person you chose, and listen through the phone the way Julian listened through the wall: hear the whole matter before you answer. Day eight hundred thirty.

831.title: Catherine and the pope
831.hook: a young laywoman writes to the pope in Avignon and urges him back to Rome
831.carry: if you are what you should be
831.howItsDone: Catholics honor Catherine of Siena as a saint and a Doctor of the Church, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read; some Christians who speak up to leaders in church and state look to her example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the anchoress's window: Julian inside, and Margery outside it. Your line was counsel at the window. Did you get to listen to someone, really listen? Day eight hundred thirty-one.

The pope doesn't live in Rome. For a long stretch of years, the popes have lived in Avignon, in the south of France, in a great palace far from the city of Peter and Paul. In Italy, a young woman from Siena, the daughter of a wool dyer, has decided this is wrong. She holds no office. She has no title. She isn't a nun in a convent; she lives a life of prayer and service as a laywoman, one of Dominic's lay sisters, in her family's house. And she starts writing letters. To princes. To cardinals. And to the pope himself, telling him, warmly and without flinching, to come home. Today: Catherine and the pope.

Catherine of Siena couldn't easily write, the old accounts say, so she dictated. Her letters went out in Italian, the language she spoke, and they are still read today. They're bold. She calls the pope by a tender family word, something like dear father, and in the same letter tells him plainly that he must be brave, stop hesitating, and return to Rome. She doesn't flatter him. She doesn't insult him either. She speaks to him as a Christian speaking to another Christian who happens to hold enormous power, and she reminds him what that power is for. She went further than letters. She traveled to Avignon herself and spoke with him there. And the pope did return to Rome. How much of that was Catherine's doing, historians weigh differently, and the return didn't end the church's troubles; a painful split came soon after. Today the Catholic Church honors her as a saint and a Doctor of the Church. There's a saying handed down under her name, usually given in English like this: if you are what you should be, you will set the whole world on fire. It's not a slogan about being impressive. It's about being true to what you were made for. Jesus says something with the same heat in the Gospel of Luke, in the King James Bible: "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?" In these letters, Catherine's fire was ink, and honesty, and love that wouldn't stay quiet in front of power.

Here's the practice: write to someone in power. Not the whole thing; for now, just begin it in your head. Who holds power over something you care about? A local official. A school board. A manager. A landlord. Let one name come. Then find your first honest sentence, the way Catherine might: respectful, warm, and clear about what needs to change. No insults. No flattery. Just the truth, said kindly. If you pray, you can ask for courage and for the right words. If you don't, just let the sentence settle until it sounds like you. The bell holds the time.
Catherine. A laywoman from Siena who wrote and spoke to the pope in Avignon, warmly and without fear, urging him to return to Rome.
Your line: if you are what you should be. Today, send the letter, the email or the message you began, and keep it as warm and as honest as Catherine's. Day eight hundred thirty-one.

832.title: Bridget of Sweden
832.hook: a widow, mother of a large family, founder, and visionary of the passion
832.howItsDone: Catholics honor Bridget of Sweden as a saint and one of the patron saints of Europe, and Bridgettine sisters still live and pray in houses that trace back to her order.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, writing to the pope in Avignon. Your line was if you are what you should be. Did you send your honest letter? Day eight hundred thirty-two.
screen: `IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.`

segments.voice: What does a woman do when the life she built is suddenly over? In Sweden, a noblewoman has spent her married years running a household, raising a large family, serving at the royal court. Tradition says she and her husband went on pilgrimage together, and that not long after, he died. She is a widow now. Her children are growing up. She could step back into a quiet widowhood. Instead, her work is about to begin. She will found a religious order, travel to Rome and never really come home, and write down visions that people still read. Today: Bridget of Sweden.

Bridget, or Birgitta in Swedish, didn't become a nun and disappear. She became something harder to describe. After her husband's death, she gave herself to prayer, and visions came to her again and again. Her early biographers say she had one even as a child; now they filled her life. They kept returning to the passion of Christ: his suffering on the cross, and his mother Mary standing near it. Her visions were written down and gathered into books called her Revelations, full of the cross seen up close, painful and tender. She also founded a religious order, often called the Bridgettines, with a great house at Vadstena in Sweden. And like Catherine yesterday, she wrote to the popes in Avignon and urged them back to Rome. She went to Rome herself, lived there for years, and died there. One of her daughters, Catherine of Sweden, stayed with her and is honored as a saint too. The Bible pays particular attention to widows. In the Gospel of Luke, when the infant Jesus is brought to the temple, an old widow named Anna is there, and the King James Bible says she "departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Widowhood, in that picture, isn't only loss. It can be a new kind of service. The letter of James is just as blunt about everyone else's part: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction". Catholics honor Bridget as a saint and a patron of Europe. Her life holds both sides: a widow's grief, and a widow's strength.
screen: `AN ORDER, AND A HOUSE AT VADSTENA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a widow in mind. Bring to mind someone who has lost a husband or a wife. A grandparent. A neighbor. A friend's mother. Someone at church or work. It might be recent, or many years ago. Let their face come, and think about what their days are like now: the meals, the empty side of the bed, the quiet evenings. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them in your thoughts, with care. And notice if there's one small thing you could do this week: a call, a visit, a meal. The bell holds the time.
Bridget. A widow and mother of Sweden who, after her husband's death, founded an order, saw visions of the passion, and spent her last years in Rome.
Your line: a widow's strength. Today, make the call or the visit you thought of: to visit the widows in their affliction, as James puts it. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

833.title: Wycliffe's Bible
833.hook: an Oxford scholar and his followers translate the Bible into English, against the law
833.howItsDone: Christians today read the Bible in their own languages, at home and aloud in worship, and Wycliffe's translation is remembered as part of the long story of putting scripture into ordinary speech.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bridget of Sweden, whose real work began when she was widowed. Your line was a widow's strength. Who did you call or visit? Day eight hundred thirty-three.

Set the scene this way. A man stands at the edge of a field in England, leaning on his plough, while someone reads to him from a small handwritten book. The words are the Gospels. And this time he understands them, because they're in English. In his parish church, the readings come in Latin, the language of scholars and priests. He has heard about the Bible all his life. Now he's hearing it. Behind that little book stands an Oxford scholar named John Wycliffe, and the followers who carried his work on. Today: Wycliffe's Bible.

John Wycliffe taught at Oxford, and he grew convinced of something that sounds simple and was explosive: ordinary Christians should be able to read the scriptures for themselves, in their own language. He criticized the wealth of the church and argued that scripture should judge the church, not the other way around. His followers, sometimes called Lollards, set out to put the whole Bible into English. They worked from the Latin Bible the church used, and every copy was written out by hand, because printing hadn't come to England yet. Copies spread among townspeople and country folk. Church authorities in England saw danger in it: errors, divisions, unrest. Before long, making or owning a new English translation without a bishop's approval was forbidden, and some who were caught with these books were punished. Christians still weigh that history differently. Some see the church protecting people from mistakes; others see it keeping the word from them. But the hope behind the work is very old. On the day of Pentecost, in the book of Acts, a crowd from many nations hears the apostles, and the King James Bible gives their astonished question: "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Every man in his own tongue. Look back over this week, and that's the thread: Sergius sharing bread at the forest's edge, Rublev leaving a place open at the table, priests who stayed with the sick, Julian at her window, Catherine writing to the pope, Bridget beginning again as a widow. People bringing faith out to ordinary ground. Wycliffe's followers brought the book itself.

Here's the practice: read scripture in your own language, slowly. Pick one short passage. If you don't know where to start, try the opening of the Gospel of John, or a psalm. Read it once, quietly. Then read it again, out loud if you can, and let each word land as if you'd never heard it in your own language before. That ploughman in the field was hearing it that way. If you pray, you can let the words become your prayer. If you don't, just stay with whichever word stops you. The bell holds the time.
Wycliffe's Bible. The handwritten English Bible made by John Wycliffe's followers from the Latin, so ordinary people could hear scripture in their own tongue.
Your line: the ploughman's bible. Today, carry one line from your reading out into ordinary ground, a field, a kitchen, a commute, and say it over once there. Day eight hundred thirty-three.

options: keep it in Latin and explain it in sermons.

fork.reveal: Wycliffe's followers put the whole Bible into English, and handwritten copies spread among ordinary people.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old English Bible.
